description: Question: on shortwave a 14 MHz signal can be heard 2000 km away while a listener 200 km away hears nothing. How can the signal skip the near station? Data: the newest ionogram of every ionosonde in the GIRO network (Lowell Global Ionospheric Radio Observatory), as compiled by KC2G's prop.kc2g.com stations API: the F2 critical frequency foF2, its peak height hmF2, the propagation factor M(3000)F2 and MUF(3000), per station. The query is a live snapshot; stations not heard from within three hours of the newest are dropped. Idea: the secant law. A layer reflects a wave going straight up only below its critical frequency foF2 (the plasma frequency of its peak electron density, f = 9√N). A wave meeting the layer at an angle of incidence i is returned up to foF2 · sec i, so the maximum usable frequency (MUF) grows with hop distance, until the ray leaves at the horizon (about 4000 km for one hop). Steps: the stations' readings with local solar time and peak electron density (Polars); MUF against distance on a curved Earth with a mirror at hmF2 (SQL); the measured M(3000)F2 against the mirror model's sec i at 3000 km; the shortest distance at which each amateur band (3.6, 7.1, 14.1, 21.1, 28.4 MHz) is returned, per station. The aha: a band above foF2 is not returned near the transmitter at all, only beyond the distance where foF2 · sec i reaches it: that ring of silence is the skip zone, and it widens at night as foF2 falls (so radio amateurs move to lower bands after dark). Caveats: the mirror model ignores the gradual bending below the peak (real reflection is lower than hmF2) and the E layer, which can screen low angles; the curve is drawn for the layer above the station, while a real hop reflects at its midpoint; absorption (D layer, by day) limits the lowest usable frequency, not modelled; a snapshot of 15 to 25 stations, mostly in Europe; GIRO data is free for scientific use with acknowledgement; autoscaled ionograms (cs = confidence score) can be wrong. Next: open the NOAA SWPC solar flux (F10.7) to see why foF2 follows the solar cycle, or plan a path between two places with the midpoint's foF2.
name: The skip zone: why far stations hear you and near ones don't
